extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in theories of humor (psychology, philosophy, linguistics, cognitive science)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and characterize major theoretical criteria for when/why something is humorous (relief, superiority, incongruity, benign violation, linguistic/script models, evolutionary accounts, etc.). Useful for analyzing or producing humor across disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggests humor is a mechanism for pent-up emotions or tension through emotional relief; laughter serves as a homeostatic mechanism by which psychological stress is reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor relieves tension (e.g., fears); laughter and joy result from release of excess nervous energy. Used to overcome sociocultural inhibitions and reveal suppressed desires (tickling as example). Historical proponents: Spencer, Freud, Kant. Variants discuss 'strain-rest-strain-rest' pacing in drama; empirical work (Shurcliff, Zillmann & Bryant) links amusement to tension release. Anti-pattern: humor consisting only of hostility without innocuous elements may be socially unacceptable; tendentious elements often need innocuous jokework to be acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises because the laugher feels superior to the target (laughing at others' misfortunes, infirmities or absurdities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated historically with Hobbes, Plato, Aristotle. Hobbes: laughter is 'sudden glory' at feeling better than the target; circumstances evoking it include success beyond expectations, perception of defects in others, perception of defects in one's past, and conceiving absurdity abstracted from persons. Aristotle stressed combination of incongruity and hostility. Criticisms: many types of humor don't involve superiority and feelings of superiority may be distinct from the humor itself. Practical implication: jokes that rely on punching down risk ethical criticism; 'punching up' seen as more acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective disposition theory
rubrics_metrics.description: In media/entertainment, audiences make moral judgments about characters; their dispositions toward characters affect enjoyment of comedic outcomes (mirth greater when bad things happen to disliked characters and vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines: greater negative disposition toward disparaged agent => greater mirth; greater positive disposition toward target => less mirth. Disposition toward victor: negative disposition reduces mirth, positive disposition increases it. Explains why audiences enjoy comeuppance for disliked characters; also explains limits (tragedy can overpower laughter). Relevant to 'punching up/down' judgments and audience identification with comedian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory (incongruous juxtaposition / incongruity-resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor and laughter rely on incongruity—anything contrary to expectation according to some norm. Humor often requires resolving the incongruity (a cognitive shift or surprise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly instantiated in wordplay and riddles (e.g., 'black and white and read all over' => newspaper). Key elements: surprise, cognitive dissonance, and resolution of incongruity. Philosophical versions (Kant, Schopenhauer) emphasize sudden transformation of expectation; other refinements (Bergson, Latta, Boyd, Koestler) emphasize perspective shift, collision of frames, or structure-mapping. Practical note: humor can be produced by unexpected shifts of perspective; the degree or suddenness of incongruity affects intensity of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign Violation Theory (BVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor occurs when three conditions are satisfied: (1) something threatens one's sense of how the world 'ought to be'; (2) the threatening situation seems benign; (3) a person sees both interpretations at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains tickling/play-fighting (threatening but safe) and a wide set of violations (physical threats, dignity, linguistic norms, social norms, moral norms). A violation can seem benign because of competing norms, psychological distance, or weak commitment to the violated norm. Predicts individual/contextual differences in amusement (e.g., church members less amused by church-related violations). Practical implication: to be funny a violation must be construal-able as both wrong/threatening and safe/acceptable simultaneously; too much attachment to the norm eliminates benign perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script-based Semantic Theory of Humor (SSTH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal jokes work when the text is compatible with two different semantic scripts and those scripts are opposing; humor is evoked when a punch line triggers abrupt switch from primary script to secondary opposing script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raskin's two conditions: (i) the text is compatible with two different scripts; (ii) the two scripts are opposite. Example: DOCTOR vs LOVER scripts in a riddle. Script oppositions include actual/non-actual, normal/abnormal, possible/impossible, good/bad, obscene/non-obscene, money/no money, high/low stature, etc. Cultural dependence: script inventories vary by culture (e.g., Soviet political humor vs Jewish humor). Not every juxtaposition is a joke—scripts must be cleverly connected so they 'make pseudo-sense together.'

rubrics_metrics.name: General Theory of Verbal Humor (GTVH) — six Knowledge Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal humor can be modeled with six independent Knowledge Resources (KRs) which characterize and constrain jokes: Script Opposition (SO), Logical Mechanism (LM), Situation (SI), Target (TA), Narrative Strategy (NS), and Language (LA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each KR: SO = script opposition (e.g., real/unreal); LM = mechanism linking scripts (pun, faulty logic, false analogy); SI = objects/activities/props; TA = target/butt of joke (optional); NS = narrative format (narrative/dialogue/riddle); LA = wording and placement of functional elements. KRs are hierarchically ordered (higher KRs constrain lower ones). GTVH can categorize all humorous texts (not only short jokes) and measure similarity between jokes by comparing KR instantiations. Empirical testing has been attempted; KRs help analyze variants (e.g., light bulb joke variants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer model of humor (Suslov)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treats humor as an information-processing malfunction where a false version must be quickly deleted from consciousness (aligns with incongruity-resolution) and emphasizes timing and neural mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adds timing to ambiguity's role; suggests deletion of false hypothesis corresponds to zeroing part of neural network and excess neural energy is thrown to motor cortex, producing laughter. Accounts for verbal and visual humor, tickling, differences in susceptibility to humor, nervous laughter, and role of intonation. Argues humor has biological origin with social functions arising later; potential computational realization requires extensive databases and neural-network implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misattribution theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience members are unable to identify precisely what is funny and misattribute their amusement to innocuous elements while tendentious (hostile/taboo) elements drive the reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally attributed to Zillmann & Bryant (1980) and influenced by Freud. Claims that taboo/hostility evokes laughter, but people believe they laugh at innocent features; explains why victimization or hostile elements can increase amusement even if conscious perception focuses on innocuous cues. Empirical work discusses distinction between tendentious and non-tendentious humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontic-epistemic theory of humor (Marteinson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is a reaction to a cognitive impasse where social being appears no longer factual or normative—comic perception reveals factual reality contradicting social reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic cases include 'Deculturation' (factual reality disconfirms social reality) and 'Relativisation' (social reality contradicts other elements of social reality). Laughter anesthetizes and resets social perception, allowing forgetting of the comic stimulus and communicating the humorous reaction. Emphasizes epistemological difficulty and re-booting faculty of social perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection / evolutionary sexual-display theory (Geoffrey Miller)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor evolved by sexual selection as an indicator of desirable traits (e.g., intelligence); thus humor functions as a fitness display rather than having direct survival value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues humor signals cognitive/creative traits attractive in mate choice. Practical implication: humorous display may function to advertise intelligence; contrasts with accounts that assign direct survival advantage in ancestral environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of mistaken reasoning (Hurley, Dennett, Adams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor evolved because it strengthens the brain's ability to find mistakes in active belief structures—detecting mistaken reasoning and improving practical problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions humor as adaptive for cognitive error-detection and problem solving; aligns somewhat with sexual selection account insofar as detecting mistaken reasoning signals valuable cognitive skills. Uses analysis of jokes to show how humor exercises error-detection circuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as defense mechanism (Vaillant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifies humor as a level-4 defense mechanism: overt expression of ideas/feelings (especially unpleasant ones) that gives pleasure to others and enables confronting distressing topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes humor from wit (wit skirts distress by displacement). Practical implication: using humor can allow expression of painful truths in an acceptable form; suggests therapeutic and interpersonal functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of humor vs sense of seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: One must distinguish what is intended as humorous vs literal/serious; misreading can cause humor to be taken seriously (bad taste) or used to convey serious information (e.g., court jesters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological study of cues that mark humor vs seriousness; bad taste occurs when the audience takes a joke literally or crosses a social line. Practical implication for creators: provide signals to indicate humorous intent when making serious points, and be mindful of audience interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor, metonymy, and allegory approaches (Veale, Bakhtin, conceptual blending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can arise from metaphorical and metonymic mappings, conceptual blending, and poetic/allegorical transformations of protagonist/worldview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tony Veale uses structure-mapping, conceptual metaphor, and conceptual blending to formalize how metaphor/metonymy produce humor. Bakhtin emphasizes 'poetic metaphor' and allegorization in humor. Practical implication: creative use of metaphorical mapping and blending of conceptual domains can generate novel humorous effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: O'Shannon model of the comedic event
rubrics_metrics.description: A unified framework consisting of four sections—context, information, aspects of awareness, and enhancers/inhibitors—with interactions determining comedic response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: reception factors prior to comedic information. Information: cognitive processing required and degree of incongruity (predictive likelihood). Aspects of awareness: multiple simultaneous perspectives (internal reality, external role, effects on context and others). Enhancers/inhibitors: feelings (superiority, relief, aggression, identification, shock) that modulate response. Model explains variety: low incongruity wordplay may produce appreciative response; high incongruity may produce visceral response; interactions allow a joke to rely on non-incongruity enhancers like superiority or identification. Also covers evolutionary accounts and 'comedic entropy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnoticed fall-back to former behaviour patterns model
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines laughter as an acoustic signal indicating an unnoticed fall-back to earlier behaviour patterns; unifies aspects of superiority and incongruity theories and links ticklishness with humor via bipedalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats laughter as communicative signal to others that someone has reverted unknowingly to an earlier routine. Suggests a social function in correcting or marking automaticity; offers cross-connections to other theories (superiority/incongruity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bergson's theory (mechanism applied to life / rigidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic situations arise from 'mechanism applied to life'—rigidity, inflexibility, automatism, and mechanical behavior in living beings produce comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man falling, imitation, absent-mindedness, repetitive gestures, resemblance between faces. Bergson treats laughter as intellectual activity with social/moral role in enforcing uniform behaviour by condemning eccentricity. Emphasizes focus on resistance and rigidity of body/behaviour as source of comic, not ugliness per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex systems / dynamical systems approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply complex/chaos theory to humor: interacting parts of a complex system give rise to collective behaviour (humor) and change is central; offers transdisciplinary modeling of how jokes/puns/memes originate and evolve in discourse communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested pivot by Attardo (2020); applications include studies connecting incongruity/resolution dynamics to psychotherapy and modeling conversational humor emergence/decline in online communities. Practical implication: use complexity-based models to analyze humor as emergent, context-dependent, and dynamic rather than static rule-based phenomenon.
